query_text: Should electroconvulsive therapy be used as a mental health treatment?

action.query: electroconvulsive therapy clinical guidelines depression APA NICE 2024 benefits risks
queries: electroconvulsive therapy clinical guidelines depression APA NICE 2024 benefits risks
Mayo Clinic electroconvulsive therapy risks benefits

annotations.title: Depression - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)

content.text:
Yes—**electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) can be an appropriate and sometimes life-saving mental health treatment**, but it should be used **selectively**, with careful medical evaluation, informed consent, and monitoring.

ECT is not the “punitive shock therapy” often shown in movies. Modern ECT is performed under **general anesthesia**, with muscle relaxation, controlled electrical stimulation, and medical monitoring. It is most often considered for **severe major depression**, especially when depression is **treatment-resistant**, accompanied by **psychosis**, severe suicidality, catatonia, or when a rapid response is needed. It may also be used in some cases of bipolar disorder, mania, catatonia, and certain severe psychotic conditions. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/electroconvulsive-therapy/about/pac-20393894?utm_source=openai))

The strongest argument **for** ECT is that it can work quickly and effectively when medications and psychotherapy have not helped, or when waiting weeks for medication response is unsafe. NIMH notes that brain-stimulation treatments such as ECT may be used earlier when severe depression is life-threatening—for example, when someone is at high suicide risk or has stopped eating or drinking. ([nimh.nih.gov](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/depression?linkId=100000200918528&utm_source=openai))

The strongest argument **against routine or casual use** is that ECT has real risks. Common short-term effects can include headache, nausea, muscle aches, confusion, and temporary memory problems. More concerning for some patients is the possibility of **persistent memory loss**, particularly around events near the treatment period; ECT also requires anesthesia, so medical risks must be assessed. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/electroconvulsive-therapy/about/pac-20393894?utm_source=openai))

So the best answer is: **ECT should be available, but not used lightly.** It is generally most justified when the condition is severe, disabling, dangerous, or resistant to other treatments—and when the expected benefits outweigh the risks for that individual. A patient should be told about alternatives such as medication changes, psychotherapy, ketamine/esketamine where appropriate, transcranial magnetic stimulation, hospitalization, or other interventions, depending on the diagnosis and urgency.

If you’re asking for yourself or someone close to you, the right next step is a discussion with a psychiatrist who can explain: **why ECT is being recommended, what alternatives exist, what memory risks apply, whether unilateral or bilateral ECT is planned, how many sessions are expected, and what relapse-prevention plan will follow.** If there is immediate danger of suicide or inability to eat/drink, seek urgent help or emergency care.
